background.title: SL, HL and AHL: what the labels mean
background.html:
IB Chemistry is taught at two levels: SL (Standard Level) and HL (Higher Level). You take HL, so everything on this page is for you.

  • Parts with no label are for everyone, SL and HL.
  • Parts marked HL are the extra parts that only HL students learn and are tested on.
  • AHL means Additional Higher Level: the IB's own name for those extra HL parts. The class "AHL answer sheet" covers them.

Paper 1A is the multiple-choice part of the exam. The quiz at the end of this page is written in that style.

background.title: Atoms, elements and the periodic table
background.html:
Everything is made of tiny atoms. An atom has a very small nucleus in the centre, made of protons and neutrons, with electrons moving around it.

An element is a substance with only one kind of atom. There are 118 of them, listed in the periodic table in order of their number of protons, the atomic number Z: hydrogen 1, helium 2, ... calcium 20, iron 26.

  • Rows are called periods (1 to 7).
  • Columns are called groups (1 to 18). Elements in the same group behave in similar ways.

Keep a periodic table open next to this page: you need it to look up Z.

background.title: Charges and ions
background.html:
Protons are positive (+), electrons are negative (−), neutrons have no charge. Opposite charges attract and like charges repel. That attraction keeps the electrons around the nucleus.

An atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so it has no overall charge. If it loses electrons it becomes a positive ion; if it gains electrons it becomes a negative ion. The number of protons never changes.

ParticleProtonsElectrons
Na atom1111
Na+ (lost 1)1110
Cl− (gained 1)1718

background.title: Reading formulas and equations
background.html:
A formula shows which atoms are in a substance. Small low numbers (subscripts) count atoms: H2O has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom; Cl2 is a molecule of 2 chlorine atoms. No number means 1.

Small raised signs (superscripts) after a symbol show charge: Na+, O2−. A raised number in front, like 37Cl, is the mass number of one isotope.

An equation shows a change: starting substances, an arrow, then what forms. The letters in brackets are state symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. NaCl(s) → Na+(aq) + Cl−(aq) means solid salt dissolving in water to give separate ions.

background.title: Energy: moving and stored
background.html:
Energy is measured in joules (J); 1 kJ = 1000 J. Two kinds come up today:

  • Kinetic energy is the energy of movement: Ek = ½mv², where m is mass and v is speed. If two particles have the same kinetic energy, the lighter one must be moving faster.
  • Potential energy is stored energy. Particles that attract each other gain potential energy when they are pulled apart, like a stretched rubber band.

Energy taken in is absorbed; energy given out is released. In an atom, an electron further from the nucleus has more energy, like a ball higher up a staircase: it can only sit on a step, never between steps.

background.title: Light as a wave
background.html:
Light travels as a wave. Two numbers tell you about a wave:

  • Wavelength (λ, "lambda"): the distance from one peak to the next. For light it is tiny and given in nanometres (1 nm = 10−9 m). Red is about 700 nm, violet about 400 nm.
  • Frequency (f): how many waves pass a point each second, in hertz (Hz).

All light travels at the same speed, c = 3.00 × 108 m s−1, and c = λf. So a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency, and a higher frequency means more energy. Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays (longest wavelength to shortest).

background.title: Standard form and units
background.html:
Very large and very small numbers are written in standard form: a number from 1 to 10 multiplied by a power of ten.

  • 6.02 × 1023 = 602 000 000 000 000 000 000 000
  • 9.116 × 10−8 = 0.000 000 091 16

To multiply, multiply the front numbers and add the powers: (2 × 103) × (3 × 105) = 6 × 108. To divide, divide the front numbers and subtract the powers. On a calculator use the ×10x (or EXP) key, not × 1 0 ^.

A power of −1 on a unit means "per": m s−1 is metres per second, mol−1 is per mole. J s means joules multiplied by seconds.

background.title: Electron shells: the Grade 9 and 10 picture
background.html:
Before IB, electrons are drawn in circles (shells) around the nucleus. For the first 20 elements the shells fill 2, then 8, then 8, then the rest: sodium (11 electrons) is 2, 8, 1 and calcium (20) is 2, 8, 8, 2.

The electrons in the outermost shell decide how an element reacts. For groups 1 and 2 their number equals the group number: sodium has 1 outer electron and is in group 1.

S1.3 adds detail to this picture: each shell (now called a main energy level, n) is split into sublevels (s, p, d, f), and each sublevel into orbitals. Sodium's 2, 8, 1 becomes 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹: the same 2, then 2 + 6 = 8, then 1.

background.title: Averages and weighted averages
background.html:
A normal average adds the values and divides by how many there are. A weighted average lets the more common values count more.

Example: a bag has 3 marbles of 10 g and 1 marble of 14 g. The average marble mass is (3 × 10 + 1 × 14) ÷ 4 = 11 g. It is closer to 10 g because most of the marbles are 10 g.

With percentages: 75% at 10 g and 25% at 14 g gives (75 × 10 + 25 × 14) ÷ 100 = 11 g, the same answer. This is exactly how relative atomic mass (Ar) is worked out from isotope masses and their percentage abundances.

terms.def: Give reasons or causes: say why or how, not just what. As an IB command term it means a detailed account with reasons, usually worth more than one mark.
To say what something is like or what happens. As an IB command term: give a detailed account. Reasons are not needed (that would be "explain").
IB command term "state": give a specific name, value or other short answer. No explanation or working is needed.
IB command term: get a number as the answer and show the working steps. A right answer with no working can lose marks.
IB meaning: pick out the answer from a number of possibilities, for example say which element or isotope something is.
IB command term: work out a conclusion from the information given. "Deduce the group" means use the numbers in the question to reach the answer.
IB command term: make an accurate diagram or graph with labels, in pencil (with a ruler for straight lines).
IB command term: draw a quick labelled diagram or graph that shows the general shape and main features. It does not need to be exact.
Made of particles. "The particulate nature of matter" means the idea that everything is made of tiny particles.
Anything that has mass and takes up space: every solid, liquid and gas. Light and heat are not matter.
A simplified picture or explanation of something we cannot see directly. It helps us explain and predict, even if it is not the full truth.
A tiny piece of matter, far too small to see: an atom, a molecule or an ion.
The smallest particle of an element. It has a tiny nucleus in the centre with electrons around it.
Two or more atoms bonded together as one particle. O<sub>2</sub> (two oxygen atoms) and H<sub>2</sub>O (water) are molecules.
A substance made of only one kind of atom (all its atoms have the same number of protons), such as oxygen or iron. All 118 elements are in the periodic table.
A substance made of atoms of two or more elements bonded together in a fixed ratio. Water, H<sub>2</sub>O, is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
Two or more substances mixed but not bonded together, so they can be in any amounts. Salt water is a mixture.
Held together by chemical bonds: strong attractions between atoms. To split a compound back into its elements you need a chemical reaction; filtering, boiling or other physical methods cannot do it.
How many of one thing there are compared with another. In H<sub>2</sub>O the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen atoms is 2:1, meaning 2 for every 1.
Physical means change only the form of a substance (melting, dissolving, filtering); no new substance forms. Chemical means use a chemical reaction, which makes new substances.
A property you can observe or measure without turning the substance into something new: boiling point, density, solubility, colour.
How a substance reacts with other substances. For example, sodium reacts with chlorine to make salt.
A change in which bonds break and form, so new substances are made, such as burning or rusting. Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.
Splitting a compound into simpler substances by passing electricity through it. Electrolysis of water gives hydrogen gas and oxygen gas.
One of the substances that make up a mixture. In salt water the components are salt and water.
The same all the way through. A homogeneous mixture looks like one substance: you cannot see separate parts. Salt water and air are examples.
Not the same all the way through. A heterogeneous mixture has parts you can tell apart, such as sand in water, or oil floating on water.
What something is made of and in what amounts. The composition of air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% other gases.
A part of a mixture that looks the same all through and has a clear edge with the other parts. Oil on water is two phases (two layers), sand in water is two (solid and liquid), salt water is one.
A mixture of a metal with other elements, made by melting them together. Steel (iron with a little carbon) and brass (copper with zinc) are alloys.
A hard rock made of different coloured grains you can see with your eyes, so it is a heterogeneous mixture.
The liquid that something dissolves in. In salt water, water is the solvent.
To break up into separate particles that spread through a liquid, so the solid can no longer be seen. Sugar dissolves in tea.
What you get when a substance dissolves in a solvent: a homogeneous mixture, such as salt solution (salt dissolved in water).
Does not dissolve. Sand is insoluble in water.
How much of a substance can dissolve in a solvent. Most solids dissolve more in hot water than in cold.
The temperature at which a liquid boils, turning to gas all the way through. Water's boiling point is 100 °C. Each pure substance has its own.
Small amounts of unwanted substances mixed into the substance you want.
Comes out of a solution as solid crystals: small pieces with flat faces and a regular shape, like grains of salt or sugar.
Making a substance on purpose using chemical reactions.
A gas formed from a substance that is normally a liquid or solid at room temperature, such as water vapour (steam).
Cooled so that a gas turns back into a liquid, like steam turning to drops on a cold window.
Distillation with a tall column, used to separate liquids whose boiling points are close together, such as ethanol (an alcohol, boils at 78 °C) and water (100 °C).
In chromatography, the part that stays still: here, the paper. Substances strongly attracted to it move slowly.
In chromatography, the part that moves: here, the solvent creeping up the paper and carrying the substances with it.
Do not mix. Immiscible liquids form two separate layers, like oil and water.
A glass container with a tap at the bottom. Two liquid layers settle in it and you let the bottom layer out through the tap.
How much mass is packed into a given volume. A denser liquid sinks below a less dense one. A dense nucleus has a lot of mass in a tiny space.
In chemistry, organic compounds are compounds based on carbon (usually with hydrogen), such as ethanol, oils and plastics. Nothing to do with organic food.
Dissolved in water. An aqueous solution has water as the solvent; its state symbol is (aq).
Makes use of. "What it exploits" means which difference between the substances the method uses.

terms.word: state of matter, change of state
terms.def: Whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas. A change of state is going from one to another, like ice melting into water.
The energy something has because it is moving. Faster or heavier particles have more kinetic energy.
A push or a pull. Here it means the attraction that holds particles together: stronger forces need more energy to overcome.
Attractions between separate molecules (not the bonds inside a molecule). They hold molecules together in liquids and solids and are overcome on boiling.
So small that you can ignore it.
The amount of space something takes up, measured for example in cm<sup>3</sup>.
Takes in energy from the surroundings, so the surroundings get colder. Melting ice is endothermic.
Gives out energy to the surroundings, so they get warmer. Freezing and burning are exothermic.
An atom (or group of atoms) with an electric charge because it has lost or gained electrons. Na<sup>+</sup> has lost one electron; Cl<sup>−</sup> has gained one.

A chemical equation shows a reaction or other change in symbols: starting substances on the left, an arrow, what forms on the right. NaCl(s) → Na<sup>+</sup>(aq) + Cl<sup>−</sup>(aq) is salt dissolving.
The scientific temperature scale, symbol K. It starts at absolute zero, the coldest possible temperature, so 0 K = −273 °C. There are no negative kelvin temperatures.
A graph of temperature (up the side) against time (along the bottom) while a substance is heated steadily, or cooled for a cooling curve. Flat parts show a change of state.
Escapes through a tiny hole. Lighter particles move faster, so they effuse faster.
Particles spreading out from where there are many to where there are few, like a smell spreading across a room. Lighter particles diffuse faster.
Stored energy. Here it is the energy particles have because of the forces between them: pulling them further apart increases it.
The model of the atom with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus in the centre and electrons in the mostly empty space around it.
The tiny centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons. It holds almost all of the atom's mass and is positively charged. Plural: nuclei.
The particles that atoms are made of: protons, neutrons and electrons.
A particle in the nucleus with a positive charge (+1) and a relative mass of 1. The number of protons decides which element an atom is.
A particle in the nucleus with no charge and a relative mass of 1. Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons.
A tiny particle with a negative charge (−1) that moves around outside the nucleus. Its mass is about 1/1836 of a proton's. Electrons decide how an atom reacts.
Electric charge is positive (+) or negative (−). Opposite charges attract, like charges repel. A proton has +1, an electron −1.
Mass given by comparison instead of in grams: a proton counts as 1, a neutron also about 1, and an electron almost 0 (about 1/1836).
Charge counted in units of the charge on one proton: proton +1, electron −1, neutron 0.
The number of protons plus neutrons in one atom, symbol A. Always a whole number.
The number of protons in an atom, symbol Z. It identifies the element: every atom with Z = 17 is chlorine.
Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons, so different masses. <sup>35</sup>Cl and <sup>37</sup>Cl are isotopes of chlorine.
How common something is. The % abundance of an isotope is the percentage of the element's atoms that are that isotope. "More abundant" means more common.
The average mass of an element's atoms, allowing for how common each isotope is, on a scale where a <sup>12</sup>C atom is exactly 12. Symbol A<sub>r</sub>; for chlorine it is 35.45.
An average in which the more common values count more. If 3 of 4 atoms have mass 35 and 1 has mass 37: (3 × 35 + 1 × 37) ÷ 4 = 35.5.
The Greek capital letter sigma. It means "add them all up". Here: for each isotope work out mass × % abundance, then add the results.
The digits in a number that carry meaning, counted from the first digit that is not zero. 35.48 has 4 significant figures; 0.0230 has 3.
The booklet of constants, equations and the periodic table that you are given in the IB exam.
In a mass spectrometer the detector gives an electric current that is bigger when more ions hit it. So the currents show relative abundance, but they do not add up to 100.
An instrument that turns atoms into ions and sorts them by mass. It shows which isotopes an element has and how common each one is.
The graph a mass spectrometer produces: m/z along the bottom, abundance up the side. Each peak is one kind of ion. Plural: mass spectra.
To turn an atom into an ion, here by knocking an electron off. Ionisation is this process; ionisation energy is the energy it needs.
An ion's mass divided by its charge, written m/z. For an ion with a 1+ charge, m/z is simply its mass.
The highest point of a wave. On a graph, a tall line or bump: in a mass spectrum each peak shows one kind of ion, and a taller peak means more of it.
How likely something is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), or 0% to 100%.
The chart of all the elements in order of atomic number. Rows are called periods and columns are called groups.
The light given out by an element when it is heated or has electricity passed through it. For a gas of atoms it is a set of separate coloured lines.
Something spread out in order. For light: the wavelengths in order, like a rainbow. A mass spectrum spreads ions out in order of mass. Plural: spectra.
A spectrum that shows only certain wavelengths, as separate bright lines on a dark background.
A spectrum with every wavelength and no gaps, like a rainbow where each colour blends into the next.
The distance from one wave peak to the next, symbol λ (lambda). Visible light has wavelengths of about 400 to 700 nm.
How many waves pass a point each second, symbol f, measured in hertz (Hz). Light with a higher frequency carries more energy.

Energy travelling as waves at the speed of light. From longest to shortest wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. Together these are the electromagnetic spectrum.
A triangular block of glass that splits white light into its colours.
Holding a sample in a flame and looking at the colour. Each metal gives its own colour; sodium gives orange-yellow.
An atom whose electron has moved up to a higher energy level than normal after taking in energy. It does not stay there for long.
Moved up to a higher energy level.
A tiny packet of light energy. Its energy is E = hf, so light of higher frequency is made of more energetic photons.
Gives out (here, light).
One of the fixed energies an electron in an atom is allowed to have, numbered n = 1, 2, 3 ... going outwards from the nucleus. Higher n means higher energy.
Separate and fixed, with nothing in between, like the steps of a staircase rather than a ramp.
Get closer and closer together, heading towards one point.

The point where the lines of one series in a spectrum get so close that they merge. It matches the electron being removed from the atom completely, so for the series ending at n = 1 it gives the ionisation energy.
An electron moving from one energy level to another. A fall gives out a photon; a move up needs energy to be taken in.
Ultraviolet: radiation with a shorter wavelength and higher energy than violet light. We cannot see it; it causes sunburn.
Infrared: radiation with a longer wavelength and lower energy than red light. We cannot see it, but we feel it as heat.
Infinity. n = ∞ means "infinitely far up": the electron has left the atom completely.
A smaller group of orbitals inside a main energy level, labelled s, p, d or f. Main level 2 has a 2s and a 2p sublevel.
A region around the nucleus where an electron is likely to be found. Each orbital holds at most two electrons.
A drawing of electrons in boxes: each box is one orbital, each arrow is one electron, and an up and a down arrow show opposite spins.
Which way something points. The three p orbitals point in three directions at right angles to each other: x, y and z.
Electrons fill the lowest-energy sublevel available first, like filling a building from the ground floor up. "Aufbau" is German for "building up".
In orbitals of the same energy, electrons go one per orbital, with parallel spins, before any orbital gets a pair. Like bus passengers taking empty double seats first.
An orbital can hold at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins.
A list of which sublevels an atom's electrons are in. 1s² 2s² 2p³ means 2 electrons in 1s, 2 in 2s and 3 in 2p: nitrogen, 7 electrons.
A short way to write a configuration: the noble gas before the element, in square brackets, stands for the inner electrons, then you add the rest. Iron: [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶.
Noble gases (group 18: He, Ne, Ar, Kr) have full outer s and p sublevels, a very stable arrangement. [Ar] stands for argon's 18 electrons, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶.
Small raised numbers or signs, like the ² in 1s². In a configuration they give the number of electrons in each sublevel.
A property of electrons with two possible values, drawn as an up arrow ↑ or a down arrow ↓. Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins.
Spins pointing the same way, drawn as arrows that all point up (↑ ↑ ↑).
Paired electrons share one orbital (↑↓). An unpaired electron is alone in its orbital (↑).
Shaped like a gym dumbbell or a figure of eight: two round lobes, one on each side of the centre.
The rounded parts of an orbital's shape. A p orbital has two lobes, one on each side of the nucleus.
A row of the periodic table. Elements in period 3 have their outer electrons in main energy level 3.
A column of the periodic table, numbered 1 to 18. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways.
Elements in groups 1, 2 and 13 to 18: all the elements except the transition metals in the middle of the periodic table.
The metals in the middle block of the periodic table (groups 3 to 12, such as iron and copper), where the d sublevel is being filled.
Having no overall charge: the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
Any particle you are asked about: an atom, an ion or a molecule. Fe and Fe<sup>2+</sup> are two different species.
Lower in energy, so less likely to change. The more stable arrangement is the one the atom ends up in.
The energy needed to remove electrons from atoms, making positive ions. The exact definition to learn is in 1.3.6.
Short for ionisation energy.
The chemist's counting unit: 1 mole is 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> particles, just as a dozen means 12. Symbol mol.
Kilojoules per mole: the energy for one mole of particles. mol<sup>−1</sup> means "per mole", and 1 kJ = 1000 J.
The number of particles in one mole: 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup>. Multiply a value for one atom by it to get the value for one mole.
The number h = 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s that links a photon's energy to its frequency: E = hf.
In the gas state, written (g).
Hertz, the unit of frequency: 1 Hz is one wave per second.
Nanometre: one billionth of a metre, 1 nm = 10<sup>−9</sup> m. Used for the wavelengths of light.
Inner electrons sit between the nucleus and the outer electrons and repel them, so the outer electrons feel less of the nucleus's pull.
A push apart. Particles with the same charge, such as two electrons, repel each other.
The total positive charge of the nucleus, equal to the number of protons. A bigger nuclear charge pulls the electrons more strongly.
The Grade 9 and 10 name for a main energy level (filled 2, 8, 8 ...). Inner shells are the levels closer to the nucleus.
The electrons in the highest main energy level that has electrons in it, furthest from the nucleus. They are the ones lost or shared in reactions.
One after another, in order. Successive ionisation energies are for removing the 1st, then 2nd, then 3rd ... electron.
An order of magnitude is a factor of 10. Values covering several orders of magnitude go from, say, hundreds to tens of thousands.
A graph scale where each equal step multiplies by 10 (1, 10, 100, 1000) instead of adding. It lets small and very large values fit on one graph.
Must be included: you lose the mark without it.
Tested in the exam. "Not assessed" means you will not be asked about it.
IB meaning: make clear how two or more things are different. For example, say what makes a compound different from a mixture.
IB meaning: use what you know to spot patterns in given information (a graph, a spectrum, a table) and say what they show.
IB meaning: give the exact meaning of a word or idea. Definitions are often marked word by word, so learn them exactly.
IB meaning: use a rule or idea to solve a given problem. Here: use the three rules to work out where the electrons go.
Show how two or more things are linked. For example: shorter wavelength goes with higher frequency and more energy.
Change a value into a different unit, for example from °C to K.
The model that all matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving. How fast they move and how strongly they attract each other decide whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas.
The way an atom or ion is written with its numbers: mass number A top left, atomic number Z bottom left, charge top right. Example: <sup>37</sup><sub>17</sub>Cl<sup>−</sup>.
Letters in brackets after a formula that show its state: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.
Higher Level, the harder version of IB Chemistry. Parts marked HL are only for HL students. SL is Standard Level. AHL (Additional Higher Level) is the IB's name for the extra HL parts.
The multiple-choice part of the IB Chemistry exam. HL students get 40 questions from SL and HL material.
The same everywhere. A uniform composition means every part of the mixture contains the same substances in the same amounts.
Dissolving: particles of a substance spread out in a solvent, each one surrounded by solvent particles. As a separation method: add a solvent that dissolves one component but not the other.
Pouring a mixture through filter paper. The liquid (and anything dissolved in it) passes through; solid pieces that are too big stay on the paper.
A liquid turning into a gas at its surface, below its boiling point. As a separation method: heat a solution until the solvent has gone, leaving the dissolved solid behind.
Making a solid purer: dissolve it in a little hot solvent, let it cool so that pure crystals form, then filter them off. The impurities stay in the liquid.
Boiling a liquid mixture and cooling the vapour so it turns back into liquid in a separate container. The substance with the lower boiling point comes off first.
Separating dissolved substances (such as the dyes in an ink) by letting a solvent creep up a strip of paper. Each substance travels a different distance.
Moving a substance out of one liquid into a second liquid that does not mix with the first and that it dissolves in better. The two layers are then separated.
In chemistry, pure means only one substance, with nothing else mixed in. Purifying means removing the other substances. Pure water contains only water.
A substance made in a chemical reaction.
The alcohol in alcoholic drinks, formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH. A liquid that boils at 78 °C.
Shake quickly back and forth around one spot without moving away from it.
Take in. Energy absorbed is energy taken in.
The lowest possible temperature, 0 K (about −273 °C). Particles have the least energy they can have.
Be in, take up. "Electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus" means that is where they are. An occupied orbital has at least one electron in it.
The negative ion of chlorine, Cl<sup>−</sup>: a chlorine atom that has gained one electron. Names ending in -ide are usually negative ions.
Be the biggest part. If <sup>7</sup>Li dominates, most lithium atoms are <sup>7</sup>Li.
Come about, happen. "How the lines arise" means what causes them.
Matches, or is the same thing as.
A general pattern in how something changes, for example ionisation energy going up as you move across a period.
A set of lines in the hydrogen spectrum made by electrons falling to the same lower level. Falls to n = 1 give one series (UV), falls to n = 2 another (visible).
Having the same energy. The three p orbitals of one sublevel are degenerate.
Shaped like a ball (a sphere).
Plural of axis: the lines x, y and z at right angles to each other, used to show directions in space.
